issues.failure_explanation: From the weak condition, at the stated threshold r = ||x-x'||^2 = (1-alpha)/(alpha*gamma) one only has ||T(x)-T(x')||^2 >= alpha^2 r - (1-alpha^2) and <= (1/alpha^2) r + (1/alpha^2 - 1). For alpha=0.9, gamma=0.1 (r=1.11) these equal 0.71 and 1.61, while the proposition claims alpha(1-gamma) r = 0.90 and (1/alpha+gamma) r = 1.35 — both violated. In general the claimed lower bound would require alpha(alpha-1+gamma) r >= (1-alpha)(1+alpha), i.e. a threshold r >= (1-alpha^2)/(alpha(gamma-1+alpha)) strictly larger than the stated one; when gamma <= 1-alpha the claimed lower bound is unattainable for every r, and the upper bound similarly needs a strictly larger threshold. No proof is given.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Correct the separation threshold (e.g. r >= (1-alpha^2)/(alpha(gamma-(1-alpha))) for the lower bound and the analogous threshold for the upper bound, restricting gamma > 1-alpha), or weaken the stated constants.
issues.overall_effect: The asserted implication that weak alpha-bi-Lipschitz control yields the regular bi-Lipschitz condition on well-separated pairs (also restated in prose in Section 3.1) is false as stated. No labelled result relies on it.
issues.title: Weak-to-strong bi-Lipschitz proposition is false at the stated separation threshold
issues.why_classification: Routine local correction of constants/threshold; the qualitative message survives and no downstream result is affected.

Example: on M=[0,1], T_n(x)=int_0^x g_n with g_n=1 on [0,1/2] and 1/n on (1/2,1] are injective, 1-Lipschitz, vanish at 0, yet converge uniformly to a map constant on [1/2,1]. issues.failure_explanation: The second variation depends on h only through its values on T(M), a compact proper subset of R^d. Any h supported off T(M) has delta^2 L_rec(h,h) = 0 while the claimed lower bound alpha^d c_min rho_min ||h||^2_{L^2(R^d)} is positive, so the lower bound (strong convexity) and the uniqueness conclusion fail for every d >= k. For d > k the proof's premise itself is false: T#mu is singular with respect to Lebesgue measure on R^d (T(M) is k-dimensional, hence null), the density rho_T does not exist, the d x d Gram determinant in the change of variables vanishes identically, and the upper bound also fails (h nonzero only on the null set T(M) has zero L^2(R^d)-norm but positive second variation). The false premise is Section 2's inference that a diffeomorphism M -> supp(T#mu) makes T#mu absolutely continuous on R^d; moreover, when M is a boundaryless compact k-manifold, d = k is not even admissible (no injective continuous map M -> R^k exists, by invariance of domain), so d > k is the forced regime.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restate both results with respect to the intrinsic norm on the image, e.g. ||h||_{L^2(T(M),H^k)} (or L^2(T#mu)): via the area formula delta^2 L_rec lies between alpha^k c_min rho_min ||h||^2 and alpha^{-k} c_max rho_max ||h||^2 for all d >= k, with uniqueness on T(M) up to the kernel; replace exponents alpha^d by alpha^k and state the GD rate in that (semi)norm.

issues.failure_explanation: The step bounds gamma(M^2 \ A) by rho_max nu_max times the Lebesgue measure of M^2 \ A, which requires the plan gamma to be absolutely continuous with respect to L^2 with bounded density. But gamma's first marginal is the discrete empirical measure mu_hat_n (and optimal couplings of even continuous marginals are typically singular), so gamma(A^c) is not controlled by L^2(A^c): atoms can have atypical bad sections and the plan's conditionals can concentrate on them. The lemma, which must hold for the defined (arbitrary) plan, is therefore false in general — a plan in Pi(mu_hat_n, nu) concentrating one atom's conditional on a bad section has gamma(A^c) >= 1/n however small L^2(A^c) is. The GME cost controls the distortion only in mu^2-average, which is invisible to such singular plans.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified; at minimum, a repair must control the plan's mass of the distortion set for the specific (optimal, singular) couplings actually used — e.g. via second-marginal section bounds, which cost at least an n-fold degradation of the epsilon_GME term and weaker probability guarantees — or restructure the argument (e.g. regularized transport), which is new analysis.
